item.title: Dutch asylum numbers a third lower than a year ago
item.description:
Dutch asylum numbers a third lower than a year ago

September 17, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The number of people registering for asylum in the Netherlands has fallen below 600 a week for the first time this year, according to weekly figures from the asylum ministry.

The drop is heavy compared to last year, when for most of autumn 2025 the weekly total was around 1,000, Volkskrant reported on Thursday.

The drop in numbers is mostly down to a reduction in family reunification requests. The number of relatives arriving to join people who already have refugee status has dropped from around 300 a week before the summer to between 110 and 120 a week over the past fortnight.

Syrians
The Netherlands has recorded more than 40,000 asylum-related arrivals every year since 2022. New applications fell sharply after the collapse of the Assad regime in Syria in December 2024, but the total stayed roughly level because Syrians who already had refugee status were still bringing over their families.

A record 16,500 family members arrived in 2025, up 39% on the year before, and three-quarters of them were Syrian, according to statistics agency CBS.

Tighter EU rules on family reunification came into force in June under the European migration pact. The ministry has not yet said what is behind the drop.

Senate
The ministry has only published a breakdown of the weekly figures since late June. Until then its weekly press release was a single line giving one total for new applications, repeat applications, resettlement and family members combined.

Applications are reportedly falling across Europe. The EU asylum agency EUAA said last week that the 27 member states plus Norway and Switzerland received 332,000 applications in the first half of 2026, 17% fewer than a year earlier and the lowest first-half total since 2021.

The agency attributed much of the drop to fewer applications from Venezuelans and Syrians.

item.title: Nearly a quarter of children in NL have divorced parents
item.description:
Nearly a quarter of children in NL have divorced parents

September 17, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

New research shows that 24% of 15-year-olds have parents who are no longer together, just a slight increase from a decade ago, according to statistics bureau CBS.

In 2025, 3.3 million children were living in the Netherlands. Around 782,000 had parents who are separated.

Twenty years ago, around 13% of 15-year-olds had divorced parents. That number increased steadily, reaching 23% in 2016, when it plateaued.

Most children of separated parents lived with their mother, particularly the youngest: 93% of 4-year-olds, falling to 83% by the age of 17.

Since 1995, the number of children with same-sex parents has also increased. In 1995, around 1,000 children had two legal mothers. By 2025, that number was more than 12,000. There are far fewer children with two legal fathers, just 500 in 2025.

The number of parents who never marry has increased sharply in the last 30 years. In 1995, of 15-year-olds with two legal parents, 80% lived with their married legal parents. Only 1,500 children of that age lived with unmarried parents.

By 2025, that share had fallen to 54.7%.

item.title: Unemployment virtually unchanged in August
item.description:
Unemployment virtually unchanged in August 

September 17, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The unemployment rate remained at 4% in August, the same as July, with around 408,000 people out of work, according to new figures from Dutch statistics bureau CBS.

While the total number of unemployed people in the Netherlands has risen, on average, by around 3,000 per month since June, the number of people leaving the labour force has also increased.

During the same time period, the number of people outside the labour force decreased by an average of 4,000 per month. Retirees and those who are unable to work due to disability or illness make up the majority of the non-labour force.

Since 2023, the number of unemployed people in the Netherlands has been slowly rising. In April, 343,000 were unemployed.

The Dutch unemployment agency UWV registered around 195,000 people on unemployment benefits. That was slightly higher, around 1.4%, than it was in July.

item.title: Netherlands slips again in global gender equality ranking
item.description:
Netherlands slips again in global gender equality ranking

September 17, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Netherlands has fallen three places to 46th out of 145 countries in the World Economic Forum’s Global Gender Gap Index, a year after dropping 15 places to 43rd.

The annual index measures the gap between men and women on economic participation, education, health and political influence.

The Netherlands has closed 75% of its gap, down 0.6 percentage points on last year, according to the University of Amsterdam team that compiled the Dutch data.

There is no longer a gap in education or health and the economic score has risen slightly, but neighbouring countries are moving faster, Henk Volberda, the UvA professor who led the research, told broadcaster NOS.

The main drag is politics: the share of women in parliament rose slightly but the number of women ministers fell, and the country has never had a female prime minister.

“I thought we had hit rock bottom last year,” Volberda said. He argued that nobody in government feels responsible for the issue, which sits with the education ministry, and wants quotas for senior public and corporate posts along with Scandinavian-style free childcare and longer maternity leave.

Iceland tops the ranking, followed by Finland, Norway, Namibia and the UK. Germany is ninth. The Netherlands was in the top 15 almost every year between 2006 and 2016.

item.title: Opposition urge cabinet to pick a route as budget debate begins
item.description:
Opposition urge cabinet to pick a route as budget debate begins

September 16, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The left-wing opposition party Pro is willing to talk to the coalition parties about reducing healthcare costs, but only if the cabinet abandons its €6.5 billion cuts to welfare spending, party leader Jesse Klaver said on the first day of the Dutch budget debate.

Klaver said it would be a “scandal” if the government fell over its first budget, but he also pressed Rob Jetten’s administration to make up its mind whether to seek support from left or right.

As the first speaker in the two-day debate on finance minister Eelco Heinen’s budget, Klaver said his party wanted to break the deadlock that led to pre-budget talks breaking down.

“After so much political unrest in recent years, I think it is in all our interests that this cabinet succeeds,” he said. “Sometimes I think the opposition is keener to make it a success than the coalition parties themselves.”

Jan Paternotte, leader of the largest coalition party D66, called on parties on all sides to work on a budget with broad appeal and look beyond “the left-right discussion in The Hague”.

But his words found little support from the opposition, which accused the coalition of D66, CDA and VVD of lacking leadership. “What kind of road map does the cabinet see before it?” Mirjam Bikker, leader of the ChristenUnie, asked.

The three parties have 66 seats in the lower house, 10 short of a majority, while in the Senate they need to find 16 extra votes to pass their legislation.

No perfect match

Pro, with 20 seats in the lower house and 14 senators, provides the most straightforward route, but the right-wing VVD is reluctant to make too many concessions to the left and favours a deal with parties such as JA21 and the orthodox Protestant SGP.

Paternotte said the coalition wanted to continue talking to parties on all sides in the coming weeks. “The perfect political match doesn’t exist, only the will to come to an agreement. My invitation stands.”

Klaver himself came in for criticism from other opposition leaders who said the proposed budget deal had already made too many concessions to the left.

Joost Eerdmans, leader of the hardline conservative JA21, said the cabinet needed to “make the choice” between his party and Pro rather than trying to reach out to both.

In contrast to Pro, JA21 argues the cabinet should cut even more from the welfare bill to create room in the budget for tax cuts and measures to ease the cost of living.

Eerdmans also said plans to invest billions in climate change measures should be redirected to help working families. “The idea that we can change the world’s climate is unrealistic,” he said.

Two budgets

Eerdmans suggested to Paternotte that the cabinet should write two budgets, one for the left-wing parties and one for the right, and let MPs debate them both.

But Paternotte urged Eerdmans to “take off the rose-tinted glasses”. “How does that get you to a majority in the Senate?” he said. “Pro or JA21 on their own aren’t enough.”

Klaver’s pitch to the cabinet also prompted Socialist Party leader Jimmy Dijk to ask how far Pro was willing to compromise on healthcare spending.

Pro would not “work to break things down”, Klaver replied, but he saw potential to make savings by tackling “all kinds of treatments that aren’t necessary” and “taking the market out of youth care”.

Draft published

Paternotte also said D66 was willing to discuss surrogate parenthood with the  SGP, which wants the cabinet to block any moves to legalise the practice as a condition for its support.

MPs also voted to ask the cabinet to publish the original draft budget by finance minister Eelco Heinen which was rejected by his coalition partners, prompting an extra weekend of negotiations.

NRC reported that the original version preserved most of the plans to cut welfare spending, despite Pro pressing for them to be taken off the table. In both the draft and the final version Heinen proposed delaying around half the cuts by a year.

item.title: Unpublished princess Diana memorial books stolen in NL
item.description:
Unpublished princess Diana memorial books stolen in NL

September 16, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Copies of an unpublished book about Diana, princess of Wales, written by her brother Earl Spencer, have been stolen from a truck in the Netherlands.

Four copies of the book, which was en route from a printing plant to a warehouse, were taken while the truck driver was sleeping in his cab in a car park, according to the BBC. Dutch publisher Overamstel has the rights to the book in the Netherlands.

The book, titled Swan Song: Diana, My Sister is highly anticipated as it is said to contain details about her personal life and unhappy marriage to then prince Charles, now the king. It also describes the crisis in the royal family that followed her death.

A source told British paper the Daily Mail that the theft was highly suspicious. “Nothing like this has ever happened before. This is probably the biggest book of the year and the security surrounding it has been incredibly tight.”

“Every possible precaution has been taken to prevent it from being leaked ahead of its serialisation. Therefore this unprecedented incident is being taken extremely seriously.”

The Dutch police are reportedly investigating the theft.

item.title: Seven men arrested as police step up illegal fireworks crackdown
item.description:
Seven men arrested as police step up illegal fireworks crackdown

September 16, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Seven men have been arrested after police intercepted several consignments of illegal fireworks from Germany over the weekend.

The suspects, aged between 31 and 60, were stopped while transporting 2,600kg of explosives to Arnhem, Heijen and Urk on Saturday.

Police said the fireworks were in the most restricted category, F4, intended for professional use only, which were already illegal before a wider ban on importing and possessing fireworks came into force on August 1.

Only the lightest category, which includes sparklers and Roman candles, will be allowed from this year, following years of campaigning by doctors and emergency services.

Police have said they will adopt a zero tolerance approach to illegal explosives in the run-up to New Year, including monitoring border crossings and checking vehicles that have been used in the past to import fireworks.

Last month a 22-year-old man from Oss was arrested after police seized a consignment of 1,200kg of fireworks in Schaijk, Noord-Brabant, one of the first major hauls since the ban took effect.

item.title: Kosovo ex-president Thaci jailed for 25 years by Hague court
item.description:
Kosovo ex-president Thaci jailed for 25 years by Hague court

September 16, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Former Kosovo president Hashim Thaci has been sentenced to 25 years in prison by a court in The Hague for war crimes committed during the 1998–99 war with Serbia, prompting clashes between his supporters and riot police in the city.

The court is an EU-backed tribunal operating under Kosovan law, and found Thaci (58) guilty of the murder of 96 people, the arbitrary detention of at least 385, and for torturing at least 303 and cruel treatment of at least 49.

The victims were largely political opponents and civilians regarded as collaborators by the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA), the ethnic Albanian guerrilla movement he led.

Three other former KLA commanders were also convicted today – Jakup Krasniqi was sentenced to 25 years, Kadri Veseli to 18 and Rexhep Selimi to 13.

All four were cleared of six counts of crimes against humanity, with judges saying prosecutors had not shown the crimes were part of a widespread and systematic attack on civilians.

Prosecutors had asked for 45-year sentences. All four men denied the charges and both sides can appeal.

Clashes on the Malieveld
Dozens of Thaci supporters had gathered on the Malieveld ahead of the verdict, and the protest turned violent shortly after it was read out.

Demonstrators threw stones, branches and flagpoles at police vans and officers, and several climbed onto a police vehicle, news agency ANP reported. Riot police used tear gas and a water cannon to disperse the crowd.

Thaci served as Kosovo’s prime minister and then president between 2008 and 2020, and helped set up the court while foreign minister in 2015.

He resigned in November 2020 to face the charges and has been in custody since. Tens of thousands of people rallied in Pristina in the days before the verdict, where the four men are widely seen as national heroes. Thaci faces a separate trial on witness intimidation charges later this month.

item.title: Suspects in Overasselt raid held in custody for another 90 days
item.description:
Suspects in Overasselt raid held in custody for another 90 days

September 16, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A court has ordered 14 people who were arrested in the aftermath of a shooting in a village near Arnhem to be kept in custody for another 90 days while inquiries continue.

Police arrested 35 people after a group of armed men descended on Overasselt in the early hours of September 1 and opened fire on a farmhouse, killing a 51-year-old guard and seriously injuring two police officers.

The suspects, who had various nationalities including French, Belgian and Algerian, were caught hiding in fields or as they tried to flee by car or train.

Military police later recovered weapons that had been abandoned at the scene, including one location near a primary school.

More suspects are due to appear in court on Wednesday and Thursday, when a judge will be asked to extend their detention. The group is accused of murder or attempted murder of the guard and attempted murder of the police officers.

It is suspected the attack was part of a feud over cocaine dealing linked with the man living in the farmhouse, Jan G., who has been targeted in the past.

Local mayor Joerie Minses has ordered G. to stay out of the village for the next three months.

item.title: Five reasons you might unexpectedly need a temporary Dutch home
item.description:
Partner content

Five reasons you might unexpectedly need a temporary Dutch home

September 16, 2026

A new job, a burst pipe, a divorce, a renovation gone on too long: there are more moments than you’d imagine when you might suddenly need somewhere to live. Here’s how serviced and flexible housing can step in, whatever the reason.

1. The new job or the temporary assignment
Relocating for work is the classic reason many people need a home in the Netherlands, but it’s far from the only version of it. Travelling nurses posted to a new hospital, researchers starting a fellowship, or consultants sent in for a few months on a project all arrive in the same position: they need somewhere to live, quickly, without signing up for a permanent rental contract.

Corporate Housing Factory (CHF) provides fully serviced apartments across the Netherlands – offering comfortable, home-style living for stays from one week up to a year, combining the convenience of a hotel with the privacy and space of a residence.

You request a quote, the team confirms availability, and in some cases you can get the keys as soon as the next day. Apartments come fully furnished, from kitchen appliances to Wi-Fi, with cleaning included. Companies are invoiced directly, and the booking system is connected to the Global Distribution System (GDS), so travel management companies can book on a client’s behalf just as easily as they could book a hotel.

CHF’s newest property, in Arnhem, is a case in point. The building dates back to 1878 and survived the bombing of the Second World War – one apartment still has a shrapnel hole, deliberately unfilled. It’s since been transformed into an industrial-chic block with high ceilings and top-quality furniture, right by Arnhem Centraal station and a local supermarket. The location was chosen for the wider Nijmegen-Arnhem-Wageningen region, where technology, healthcare, sustainability and logistics employers have long struggled to find decent corporate housing for their staff.

2. The housing emergency
Then there’s the reason nobody plans for: a fire, a mould problem, a burst pipe or damage that suddenly makes your own home unliveable. It’s the kind of situation that can leave the victim feeling like an emergency bunker is the only option. And after an already stressful event, most people would rather not compromise on comfort.

This is where Thuis in de Stad comes in: “Until recently, we focused on corporate clients, so it was always relocations, work trips or internships,” says Claudia Vrancken from CHF. “With Thuis in de Stad, we’re opening the spectrum more broadly to the other unexpected reasons someone might suddenly need temporary housing.” You can anticipate fully furnished apartments, all utilities included; arrive with a suitcase and the rest is taken care of.

3. The renovation project, or getting caught between selling and buying
The same goes for two other reasons someone might need to move out temporarily: a renovation that makes the house unliveable for a few weeks, or the gap between selling one home and getting the keys to the next. Neither is an emergency, but both mean needing a comfortable base at short notice, for an unpredictable length of time.

One detail that matters more than people expect in the Netherlands is the ability to register at an address – something most short-term rentals don’t allow, but which is essential for things like getting a BSN number or opening a bank account. (Just don’t forget to deregister when you leave!)

4. The divorce process
Separation is another situation that can leave someone needing a home almost overnight – often with the condition of staying close to children and family during a period of transition. Flexible, furnished housing means not having to make a long-term commitment while things are still being worked out, while still having a proper place to call home in the meantime.

It’s also worth knowing, whatever the reason for the move, that pets are welcome – unlike with most hotels or holiday rentals. “Our apartments are all located in mixed-use buildings, so you really have the feeling you’re living somewhere with local families, kids and pets, instead of in a hotel,” says Claudia.

5. The sudden business trip elsewhere in Europe
Not every unexpected need for a home happens in the Netherlands. A consultant might have to jump on a plane at short notice for a project in another European city, with everything needing to be arranged just as quickly as it would be here.

For that, there’s Your Serviced Apartment Agency (YOSAA): a boutique Europe-wide apartments platform. The general idea of YOSAA – connecting living, hospitality and real estate – is the same as CHF and Thuis in de Stad: the convenience of a hotel with the freedom and flexibility of your own apartment.

Whatever the reason – a new job, an emergency or a sudden change of plans – temporary housing isn’t just for expats. Sometimes life itself creates the need for a home between homes. If that sounds like you, contact the booking team via email at bookings@corporatehousingfactory.com to find the right temporary home for your situation.
